dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the instrument count sheet and closing stale entries.
The theatre roster review wrapped early today.
Standard cases up to four hours are completely unremarkable for my legs.
Someone new shadowed me in the operating theatre this morning.
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the case lengths into one message before lunch.
My circulation issue stays silent through long cases as long as position changes happen on schedule; the vascular list proved the protocol works when relief timing is honored.
The protocol is proven under real load.
With compression stockings and scheduled position changes, even a six-hour vascular case went fine last month.
I archived last cycle's notes on the theatre roster and set up the new folder.
As fresh as these things get.
My vascular specialist's letter conditions long-case participation on scheduled position-change windows.
A vendor call about the instrument count sheet ran long but ended well.
I walked through the operating theatre checklist with the new starter.
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the case lengths.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the theatre roster records and fixed it at the source.
The transplant team's marathon cases run nine hours and more, and their roster currently has no relief scrub coverage; the one nine-hour case I scrubbed uncovered ended with two days of leg swelling.
Uncovered marathon cases are the specific hazard.
I sketched next week's plan for the case lengths before leaving.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the instrument count sheet updates.
The transplant program is recruiting for its scrub pool this month, decision required by Friday.
The deadline forces the terms question.
I compared two options for the theatre roster tooling and noted a mild preference.
I closed the week by updating the operating theatre handover notes.
The transplant team asked me to join their scrub pool. What should I require before saying yes?
